Where are they now? - Iconic Ads

By: Sophia Phirippides | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
As the new South Africa emerged in the early 90’s so did the golden age of commercials –where are those familiar characters now and the creative minds that made sure we never forgot them?

Unique Selling Point:
1995, A new South Africa, an open invitation for big brands and advertising’s brain power to unleash their genius on a country braving a new world. And so they did, defining and capturing culture, challenging and questioning our perspectives through commercials with characters that made us see ourselves - creating definitive cultural moments. We reunite the team that gave us the iconic “Yebo Gogo” ads, captured in a unique Carte Blanche moment 27 years later. Where are they now, and a glimpse into their journey that made them iconic characters on our screens.

Summary:
The emergence of the “New South Africa” in the early to mid 90’s, meant that in the land of advertising, the playing field had just opened up. An inclusive country where big brands could capture new customers and define the ethos of their brand through definitive cultural moments. Two campaigns that stand out are Sasol’s Amagluglug and Vodacom’s Yebo Gogo commercials. These campaigns were so well received and entrenched that they were like running soapies, spanning several years on our tv screens.

Carte Blanche tracks down some of those iconic characters, and where they are now, as well as the creative minds that made the brands and characters household names.

Further information:
The evolution of our psyche as a country is characterised in those commercials, especially Vodacom’s “Yebo Gogo” campaign that lasted 10 years. The Brains behind it, creative director, Francois De Villiers and director Michael Middleton give us some insight and funny stories. We meet one half of the team Michael De Pinna, who played the jewish bagel, yuppie, we were unable to locate BanKole “Kole” Omotoso – who is an intellectual, professional writer and a former professor in the Drama department at Stellenbosch university. Known as the Yebo Gogo Man, apparently he now lives in Nigeria.

We reunite some of the team, in a moment captured only by Carte Blanche, where they relive some of those times and bring us to the present.

I would like this to be done with the presenter and the 3 or 4 of them around a table, quite live and interactive.. so the humour and recollection is spontaneous. Michael De Pinna is a well known actor and comedian and he is very funny on the fly. Francois loves to tell a good story, and he believes director Michael Middleton and Producer Peter Gerd were the driving creative forces that gave those commercials the longevity that they had. (Michael and Peter are in Cape Town).

A bit of background on Michael De Pinna. He’s done lots on SABC and hosted several shows
He’s friends with Carolyn Steyn.
https://www.tvsa.co.za/actors/viewactor.aspx?actorid=8652
He’s a firm believer in the paranormal and psychic studies – hosting the show Paranormal on SABC2 and studying at the college of Psychic Studies in the UK. This belief was passed down to him from his Russian grandmother.

Our next blockbuster commercial that we feature is the Sasol “Amagluglug” campaign. We tracked down Tayla Farrell, now Hutchings, who was the baby. She’s lived quite an ordinary life after achieving superstardom as the amagluglug baby, but she says that it has always been a part of her life, and her claim to fame.

Tayla matriculated at Brecia house in 2013. She then went to Culinary school in 2015-2016, she specialised in deserts. She worked at the Saxon 500 under David Higgs, and at the Palazzo. She was the head chef in Nelspruit on an avo farm for a private family – she turned to the events industry – but was retrenched during covid.

She’s now had her second child who’s 6 months old, so she’s currently a stay at home mom. Her husband is a pilot. She is really happy to participate.

She tells the funny story of how she was cast for the commercial. She was 20 months when she was spotted at a shopping centre where the agency approached her parents and recruited her. Tayla was wearing blue and they mistakenly thought she was a boy, and only on the day of filming did the director discover that he was a 'she.'

According to Francois De Villiers, the baby in the pram ad was created for a white target market, and at the same time another amagluglug ad was created for the black market. The Taxi rank one, “Windie Windie” with well know actor and comedian Desmond Dube, who has starred in many shows as well as currently doing insurance commercials. The interesting thing that emerged from those ads was that the black audiences apparently loved the pram commercial and the white audiences loved the taxi commercial. Francois expands on this interesting reversal.

We have not tracked down Desmond Dube as yet, but I think it would be amazing if we could get him. I have connected with Director and creator of all the ads Les Sharpe, who moved to Australia many years ago. Apparently he will be in Cape Town in the next week, so we could get him on camera or on zoom.

In terms of treatment, I think we could take the mickey a little with the links, and make them feel commercialsy… I wanted to do them in 4 x 3 format and move into a 16: 9 in the same link… from old to new. The links script should be a bit cheesy and reminiscent, or retro.

I also thought as part of the character intros we could ask them all for pictures of themselves at the time, and then we take a similar pose of them now and morph the old into the now. With Tayla, I thought we could meet her through her baby in a pram.. and link as to where we are now.

Les can expand on why the Amagluglug campaign was so defining and the roads it opened up for him as a director, and what he’s doing now in Australia.

The whole piece will have a retro 90’s feel when talking about the past and then come into modern 16:9 glossy feel when we’re in the now.

There are many funny and entertaining stories and characters around these commercials.

We have permission from Sasol for the “Amagluglug” ad but not yet from Vodacom. We would also need to try and source as high res versions as possible, because currently the versions I have seen are very poor quality.

Press Release:


Advertising's giants from the mid-'90s brought us some iconic ads and characters that left a lasting impression. In a special investigation, we go on the hunt to track down the characters and creatives behind the memorable Vodacom Yebo Gogo ads.

Script:


Derek: How are we doing with tracking down the cell phone guys?
Laura: We did find the guys who made it.
Derek: But most importantly the guy in the leopard skin speedo.
Laura: He's proving a little more elusive
Derek: So it looks like I'll have to do some work.

Link/ VO: I'm sure most of you remember the Yebo gogo Vodacom ads from what 27 years ago.
Derek: And guess what team, I've got hold of the main man.//
You've got to wear the leopard skin hey?
Michael: Nice try.

Link: We are going to track down all the people involved and get to the very bottom of them.
Cut to ad..skiing bottom
Up sound: Water splash
Music: Foot Steps out
VO: We reunite some of the team behind those iconic ads

Sound up: Skiing commercial

Beat// Western style the good the bad and the ugly music…
Michael's boot steps out … he surveys… slo mo
VO: The Yebo Gogo commercials had many storylines and characters spanning over a decade, and these guys were in the thick of it.
the men get out the car cut back to Michael looking
they walk up the path slow mo..
Michael: Hello guys… I said I would'nt disappoint you.
Derek: comments on the leopard skin underwear,..they all hug..
VO: Executive Creative Director Francois De Villiers, Executive Producer Peter Gird and forever imprinted in our minds, in leopard skin underwear, actor, comedian and singer Michael De Pinna.

Derek: Yebo can we go-go? I want to take you back to those years, independence was a new era for advertising.
Francois: The timing in the history of South Africa was just so right for that. We needed a fall guy. We needed a hero. Michael was the fall guy, he gets in trouble and the hero like the brand, steps in to save the day,
Peter: For the time it was so relevant, to be able to make people laugh after what we've been through.

Derek: How did you select this man?
Francois: We just saw him, he certainly had the character to be a little windgat, you know, a little bit full of himself, because then the bigger you are, the harder you can fall.
Michael: Nothing has changed. (laughter)

VO: And of course, these commercials would have fallen flat without the somewhat bemused old man, played by actor, author and Professor Bankole Omotoso.

Francois: He just had so much dignity, we just knew that he'd be perfect for our role.
Michael: Everybody wonders who said the "yebo gogo" line first and it was me.
Derek: You said you taking the credit?
Michael: I got out of the car and I went Yebo Gogo. Obviously, I got it wrong. Because Yebo gogo means yes, my grandmother.
Francois: It is actually purposely written like that it wasn't a mistake. We wanted him to get even more into trouble.

VO: So, all these years later we learn Michael was simply following instructions.

Derek: You get the call, you get the job. So there you are. But you don't know it's gonna change your life for the next decade.
Michael: I mean, people would come up to me and supermarkets and this guy came up to me and he said, I really like your ad hey, particularly and I've got some mates of mine we're gonna have a party soon, we want you to come in your tiger skin panty, and just sommer be funny.
Michael: So I said, excuse me, but if you see me in my tiger skin panty for more than 30 seconds, it ain't gonna be funny.

VO: But funny it was// And over the years thousands of South Africans became part of this epic campaign.

up sound ad…

Peter: We really went out of our way to look for members of the public who want to be actors.
VO: They even went to wrestling clubs to cast for the "real deal", remember this scene?
Sound up://

VO: It's the Naarjie commercial where Michael's onscreen girlfriend "poppy", played by actress Lauren Davies, makes the blunder of her life..
(show scene poppy throwing the nartjie)
Cut to commercial with the naartjie squelching as a transition)

LINK: These ads were just short of blockbusters, mini-movies that lit up our screens, shot in exotic and remote locations.

insert train ad Michael hanging out the window…

Francois: It was the coverage war between you know those two big networks.

VO: The last laugh, always on the " fall guy" and sometimes on the actor himself, like in the skiing ad, because Michael couldn't ski.

Michael: So I tried and I nearly drowned in a vlei, I had to hang on, I could hardly use my arms for two, three weeks after that.

Gate falling over shots of him running from the Dobermans.

VO: Sometimes he had to run away from "real" danger, and even come face to face with nature.

Shot of wave falling over his head.

Michael: And I nearly died
Francois: We purposefully didn't tell him
Peter: Well maybe we should reveal our other purposely done things.

VO: Ah, the infamous "caravan" scene.
Francois: So he comes around the corner and then he's gotta fall but he's not cracking it. Michael Middleton was our director. Okay, we're going to shift the tent peg and we don't tell him. And he hits it and he goes yaaaahhhhh.
Michael: No wonder I klapped myself so hard.

Peter: We had got the real Hells Angels to rock up at a Padstaal called Cook and Diesel. Michael took one look at this thing, went back into the caravan.

VO: So twenty-seven years later what are the members of this crack team doing now?

Peter: Oh There’s me. // So after the commercials, we looked at branded entertainment. I bring brands that we thread naturally into the content. And now, for the last year, I've been workingon probably one of the biggest reality TV shows in the world today called Young, famous and African.

Derek: Francois, it seems well, decades later, everybody is as busy or busier than before.
Francois: Still love what I'm doing. My kids are in advertising so they must think Hey, daddy had an easy job.

VO: Francois, is still working on cellphone brands, as executive creative director, but he says the advertising landscape has changed with social media….

Francois: A TV commercial those days can change a nation. Now you gotta have 1000s of relationships on social media. But your big idea for that reason has to be even bigger.

Derek: Poppy left town to what the UK? Yeah.
Francois: It was quite difficult because she was obviously a big part of it, like so many other people.
Derek: Well, we managed to track down Kole in Nigeria through his son. And you've got a message from the prof?
Francois: Sorry, I can't be with you at the reunion. But you know that yebo gogo is always in my heart.
Sound up: Hello Vodacom

Up sound: Michael singing…

VO: And what's our host been up to? // …
virtuoso actor, comedian, singer, Michael de Pinna is showing us just how entertaining re-invention can be

Cut to Michael singing his song.. Derek enters and claps!!!

Derek: Clapping: You mime so well. Okay? Cue the dog. I can see how you just love performing. It's been your life before and after the leopard skin.
Michael: I really do love performing, I perform with a wonderful singer called Hlumelo Ledwaba, who is the other half of my act And now what do I do now, I teach singers to perform and act at my school here. And there's a movie in the offing and there's also a TV commercial may be…

Derek: We hope that you keep the music playing for a long long time.
Michael: I'll do me best:
Sound Up: Michael singing

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): As the new South Africa emerged in the early 90’s so did the golden age of commercials –where are those familiar characters now and the creative minds that made sure we never forgot them?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: 1995, A new South Africa, an open invitation for big brands and advertising’s brain power to unleash their genius on a country braving a new world. And so they did, defining and capturing culture, challenging and questioning our perspectives through commercials with characters that made us see ourselves - creating definitive cultural moments. We reunite the team that gave us the iconic “Yebo Gogo” ads, captured in a unique Carte Blanche moment 27 years later. Where are they now, and a glimpse into their journey that made them iconic characters on our screens.
metadata.Summary: The emergence of the “New South Africa” in the early to mid 90’s, meant that in the land of advertising, the playing field had just opened up. An inclusive country where big brands could capture new customers and define the ethos of their brand through definitive cultural moments. Two campaigns that stand out are Sasol’s Amagluglug and Vodacom’s Yebo Gogo commercials. These campaigns were so well received and entrenched that they were like running soapies, spanning several years on our tv screens. Carte Blanche tracks down some of those iconic characters, and where they are now, as well as the creative minds that made the brands and characters household names.
metadata.Further information: The evolution of our psyche as a country is characterised in those commercials, especially Vodacom’s “Yebo Gogo” campaign that lasted 10 years. The Brains behind it, creative director, Francois De Villiers and director Michael Middleton give us some insight and funny stories. We meet one half of the team Michael De Pinna, who played the jewish bagel, yuppie, we were unable to locate BanKole “Kole” Omotoso – who is an intellectual, professional writer and a former professor in the Drama department at Stellenbosch university. Known as the Yebo Gogo Man, apparently he now lives in Nigeria. We reunite some of the team, in a moment captured only by Carte Blanche, where they relive some of those times and bring us to the present. I would like this to be done with the presenter and the 3 or 4 of them around a table, quite live and interactive.. so the humour and recollection is spontaneous. Michael De Pinna is a well known actor and comedian and he is very funny on the fly. Francois loves to tell a good story, and he believes director Michael Middleton and Producer Peter Gerd were the driving creative forces that gave those commercials the longevity that they had. (Michael and Peter are in Cape Town). A bit of background on Michael De Pinna. He’s done lots on SABC and hosted several shows He’s friends with Carolyn Steyn. https://www.tvsa.co.za/actors/viewactor.aspx?actorid=8652 He’s a firm believer in the paranormal and psychic studies – hosting the show Paranormal on SABC2 and studying at the college of Psychic Studies in the UK. This belief was passed down to him from his Russian grandmother. Our next blockbuster commercial that we feature is the Sasol “Amagluglug” campaign. We tracked down Tayla Farrell, now Hutchings, who was the baby. She’s lived quite an ordinary life after achieving superstardom as the amagluglug baby, but she says that it has always been a part of her life, and her claim to fame. Tayla matriculated at Brecia house in 2013. She then went to Culinary school in 2015-2016, she specialised in deserts. She worked at the Saxon 500 under David Higgs, and at the Palazzo. She was the head chef in Nelspruit on an avo farm for a private family – she turned to the events industry – but was retrenched during covid. She’s now had her second child who’s 6 months old, so she’s currently a stay at home mom. Her husband is a pilot. She is really happy to participate. She tells the funny story of how she was cast for the commercial. She was 20 months when she was spotted at a shopping centre where the agency approached her parents and recruited her. Tayla was wearing blue and they mistakenly thought she was a boy, and only on the day of filming did the director discover that he was a 'she.' According to Francois De Villiers, the baby in the pram ad was created for a white target market, and at the same time another amagluglug ad was created for the black market. The Taxi rank one, “Windie Windie” with well know actor and comedian Desmond Dube, who has starred in many shows as well as currently doing insurance commercials. The interesting thing that emerged from those ads was that the black audiences apparently loved the pram commercial and the white audiences loved the taxi commercial. Francois expands on this interesting reversal. We have not tracked down Desmond Dube as yet, but I think it would be amazing if we could get him. I have connected with Director and creator of all the ads Les Sharpe, who moved to Australia many years ago. Apparently he will be in Cape Town in the next week, so we could get him on camera or on zoom. In terms of treatment, I think we could take the mickey a little with the links, and make them feel commercialsy… I wanted to do them in 4 x 3 format and move into a 16: 9 in the same link… from old to new. The links script should be a bit cheesy and reminiscent, or retro. I also thought as part of the character intros we could ask them all for pictures of themselves at the time, and then we take a similar pose of them now and morph the old into the now. With Tayla, I thought we could meet her through her baby in a pram.. and link as to where we are now. Les can expand on why the Amagluglug campaign was so defining and the roads it opened up for him as a director, and what he’s doing now in Australia. The whole piece will have a retro 90’s feel when talking about the past and then come into modern 16:9 glossy feel when we’re in the now. There are many funny and entertaining stories and characters around these commercials. We have permission from Sasol for the “Amagluglug” ad but not yet from Vodacom. We would also need to try and source as high res versions as possible, because currently the versions I have seen are very poor quality. Interviews 1.
